1:
Gill sets the law in its place in the sequence: having dealt with public war, Moses turns to a private quarrel in which one man kills another. Henry sets it against the law already given. Earlier provision had been made for pursuing a wilful murderer, and putting him to death was itself the putting away of the guilt of blood from the land; the case here is what happens when that cannot be done, and his warning is that the people must not suppose the land is in no danger of pollution merely because the failure was not their fault. He allows that providence has often brought such hidden works of darkness to light, so often that it has passed into a proverb that murder will out; but not always, and now and then the devil’s promises of secrecy and impunity are made good — though only for a while, since there is a time coming when secret murders will be discovered and the earth shall disclose her blood. Wesley adds a point of scope, that the field is named not to limit the law to open country but because that is where such murders are most commonly committed; a killing in the city or anywhere else is covered.

Who goes out to measure is disputed, and Gill reports the dispute rather than settling it. Aben Ezra takes the elders and judges for those of the neighbouring cities; others make them the great council at Jerusalem, and Gill quotes the Targum for a delegation of two wise men and three judges, and the rabbinic ruling that three go out, with one authority arguing for five on the ground that thy elders means two and thy judges two, and since a court may not be even in number they add one more. Wesley reads the phrase as a single class rather than two, those of the elders who are judges, and notes that the measuring was superfluous wherever it was already evident which city lay nearest. Keil describes the procedure and the reason for it. The elders come as representatives of the communities and the judges as administrators of right, and what they measure is the distance of the body from the towns lying round it, to establish which is nearest; and the nearest town bears the expiation not only because suspicion of the crime, or of complicity in it, falls soonest there, but because the guilt of innocent blood rests as a burden on it before all others. Calvin states the principle the whole rite rests on. The law informs us how precious to God the life of man is, since where a murder has been committed by some unknown hand he still requires an expiation by which the neighbouring cities purge themselves; from which it appears that the earth is so polluted by human blood that those who encourage murder by leaving it unpunished implicate themselves in the guilt. The guilt of a secret crime attaches to the cities nearest until a diligent inquiry lets them testify that the author cannot be discovered — and if that is so, he asks, how much less excusable are they who let a murderer they could have caught escape?
3: On the heifer the descriptions agree and the interpretations do not. Keil specifies an animal with which no work had been done and which had never drawn in the yoke, that is, whose vital force had not been diminished by labour, brought down to a valley with water constantly flowing and there killed by breaking the neck. Clarke reads the Hebrew for the place as possibly a rapid stream running through uncultivated ground, and explains the requirement that the ground be untilled by what he takes the rite to be — a sacrifice made to atone for the murder, which would therefore pollute the land it was made on. Henry denies exactly that. This was not a sacrifice, he says, for it was not brought to the altar; it was a solemn protestation that thus they would have put the murderer to death had they had him in their hands, the unyoked heifer signifying, on one reading, that the murderer was a son of Belial, and the rough valley signifying both the horror of the deed and the way blood-guilt turns a land to barrenness — and he passes on the tradition that the valley was never afterwards to be tilled or sown unless the murderer was found. Calvin takes a middle position: God chose an animal that had never borne a yoke so that satisfaction made by innocent blood might be represented the more vividly, and had it killed in a desert place so that the pollution might be carried away from cultivated ground. Clarke adds a practical motive that none of the others mention, that the whole regulation was calculated to keep murder in abhorrence and to make magistrates alert in their office, so that offenders might be discovered and public expense saved. Wesley reads the same details morally and then typologically: the desert and horrid place was to beget a horror of murder, and the striking off of the neck showed what they would have done to the murderer; the beast that would not bear the yoke fitly represents the man who would not bear the yoke of God’s laws, and is at the same time a type of Christ, who was under a yoke he had voluntarily taken on himself. Gill reads the valley the same way, as an emblem of the low estate into which Christ came.
5:
The priests are brought in with care about what they are and are not there to do. Keil says some priests from the nearest Levitical town were to be present, not to conduct the affair, but as men whom the Lord had chosen to serve him and to bless in his name, and according to whose word every dispute and every stroke was decided; they attend simply as those authorised by God, representatives of divine right, to receive the elders’ declaration and petition and to acknowledge that the act was legally valid. Gill notes a smaller point in the wording, that the sons of Levi marks men whose descent was beyond question, since there were sometimes persons in that office about whom doubt existed, and he takes these to belong to the court at Jerusalem, present to direct the performance and to determine any difficulty arising. Henry draws a conclusion about the constitution from the same verse: God being Israel’s King, his ministers must be their magistrates, and every controversy must be tried by the word of men who are the mouth of the court and learned in the laws — a privilege, he adds, that the people were bound to use. Wesley reads every controversy more widely than the case in hand, extending it to any stroke or wound given by one man to another and not only to a mortal one.

The washing of hands is explained historically, devotionally and by way of a warning. Keil takes it for a symbolic cleansing from the suspicion that anyone in the town had a part in the murder, and reads the declaration that follows as an answer to a charge: our hands did not shed this blood and our eyes did not see it, meaning neither part in the crime nor knowledge of it. Clarke says the rite was anciently used to signify that those washing were innocent of the crime in question, and adds a conjecture — that it was probably from the Jews that Pilate learned this way of expressing his innocence. Henry hears the same allusion in David’s I will wash my hands in innocency, but takes Pilate the other way: if he had any eye to this custom he wretchedly misapplied it, condemning Christ while knowing him innocent and then acquitting himself of the blood, since protestations are of no avail when the fact contradicts them. Henry also presses what the elders were actually swearing to, which is more than the bare denial — not only that they had not shed the blood but that they did not know who had, and had not knowingly concealed the murderer, helped him escape, or been in any way aiding or abetting. Calvin explains what the rite was for psychologically: the washing stirred them up the more, so that they should not protest inconsiderately in so solemn a form, since it was as though they had set the corpse before God and stood opposite it to purge away the crime.
7: On the prayer that follows, Gill notes an unsettled question of speaker: the words read as a continuation of the elders’ declaration, but the Targums and the rabbinic sources take them for the priests’. Henry assumes the priests and states the reason for a prayer at all — it might be presumed that the murderer was either one of their city or now harboured in it, so they must ask not to fare the worse for his being among them; and he turns it outward, that when we hear of the wickedness of the wicked we have need to cry earnestly for mercy on our land, emptying by our prayers the measure that others are filling by their sins. Calvin gives two motives for the petition: it might have been through their own carelessness that the man was struck down, and since the sacrilege of one man had once contaminated the whole people, they had reason to fear that vengeance might spread. He is careful about what secures the answer. God declares he will not impute the blood once the rite is duly performed, not because the heifer was a price of satisfaction to propitiate him, but because in this way the people humbly reconciled themselves and shut the door against murders to come. Wesley distinguishes the two kinds of guilt at issue, that there was no mortal guilt in the people but a ceremonial uncleanness in the land, and it was that which had to be expiated and forgiven. Gill draws the ground of the appeal out of the words themselves: the people are named as those God redeemed out of Egyptian bondage and claimed for his own, and on that footing mercy is asked — that they not be punished for a sin they were wholly ignorant of, done by someone among them whom they could not yet discover. On the closing verse he reports Aben Ezra taking the guilt of innocent blood to mean its punishment, which by this method would not be inflicted on them, since otherwise, the offender never being found, it would fall on the whole community. Keil closes the case with the point the others leave unsaid: if the murderer were discovered afterwards, the death inflicted vicariously on the animal, simply because the criminal could not be found, would still fall on him.
10:
Which war is meant is settled the same way by three of them. Gill says this is an arbitrary war, one Israel entered on its own choice or under provocation, and not a war commanded by God such as that against the seven nations, since in that one there were to be no captives at all but all were to be destroyed. Keil argues the same from the wording, that the opening formula matches the previous chapter and so refers to wars with surrounding nations after the conquest, not to the Canaanites who were to be cut off. Wesley says it in six words, enemies of other nations but not the Canaanites. Calvin reaches the point by a different road, treating the law as parallel to the rules about food: Israel had already been forbidden Canaanite wives lest the connection prove an enticement to sin, and Moses now goes further, forbidding marriage even with women taken from other nations unless a solemn rite has purified them, so that a people separated to God should not defile itself with profane marriages.

What kind of concession this is, and how far it reaches, produces the sharpest divergence. Henry calls it plainly an indulgence granted for the hardness of their hearts, given lest men denied the liberty to marry such women should take the liberty of defiling themselves with them and so trouble the camp; he assumes the soldier already has a wife and takes this one as a secondary wife. He then measures the permission against the gospel and finds it wanting on three counts — the gospel does not permit a man who has one wife to take another, since from the beginning it was not so; it forbids looking on a woman to lust after her; and it commands the mortifying of every irregular desire though it be as painful as cutting off a right hand — concluding that in this respect the law of Christ far exceeds in glory the law of Moses. Calvin makes a nearly identical judgment without the comparison: it would have been better that they abstained from such marriages altogether, but it was difficult so to restrain their lust that they should not decline from chastity in the least degree, and he adds the observation that this shows how much licence conquerors allow themselves in war, so that there is no room in them for perfect purity. What God does, on his reading, is temper his indulgence so that men in the very fervour of their lust should retain some religious affection. He is careful about the scope: the question is not of unlawful ravishment, but only of women made captives by right of war, whom conquerors have always abused with impunity because they had them in their power. Clarke states the resulting protection positively — no forcible possession was allowed even here, where by the general consent of ancient nations the woman counted as part of the spoil, and the man to whose share she fell might have her as a wife on conditions but was not permitted to use her in any inferior character. Gill reports the rabbinic view that she might be virgin, wife or widow, and Wesley suggests that the phrase about desire may be a modest expression covering more than intention, since the later verse says he had humbled her, and reads the passage as treating two cases, the man who wishes to marry her and the man who does not.
12:
On the shaving and the nails the rationales diverge completely. Keil takes both as customary signs of purification, symbols of her passing out of the state of a slave and being received into the fellowship of the covenant nation, which he finds obvious in the laying aside of the prisoner’s clothes. Clarke and Wesley make them a renunciation of religion rather than of slavery, the shaven head marking her abandonment of heathen idolatry and her becoming a proselyte; Clarke notes that the custom survived in the East, a convert’s head being shaved and the man carried through the city proclaiming the new confession. Gill records a third rationale from the rabbis that runs the opposite way, that the woman was stripped of her finery precisely to abate the ardour of her captor’s love and make her less agreeable to him. Clarke also doubts the usual rendering of the second phrase: whether the Hebrew means paring the nails or letting them grow is much disputed, and he suspects it means neither but the staining of them red with henna, a practice he traces through India and Egypt and even to the nails of mummies, and which he thinks lies behind the notice that Mephibosheth had not dressed his feet.

What the raiment of her captivity was is a small disagreement with a large consequence for the picture. Gill takes it for the beautiful garments she was wearing when captured, which tended to stir up affection and desire, and reports the rabbinic opinion that Gentile women dressed finely in war precisely to entice, so that the law makes her exchange them for old worn clothes and be less agreeable; he allows the alternative that the change was simply a token of mourning, it being customary to lay aside rich clothing for sackcloth. Wesley reads the phrase the opposite way, as the sordid raiment put upon her when she was taken captive, and Keil agrees in substance by calling them the prisoner’s clothes. On the month, Keil explains it as time to console herself for the separation from parents she had lost, so that she might forget her people and her father’s house and give herself henceforth in love to her husband; Wesley allows the mourning to be either for their death or for what came to the same thing, her final separation from them.

The release, if he tires of her, is where Calvin makes his most exact point. He says he had to detach this sentence from the passage before it, which he had expounded elsewhere, because the two belong under different heads: the earlier law concerned chastity, conjugal fidelity and the purity of God’s worship, while this one prescribes that a man who has dishonoured a captive shall not sell her but let her go free, wiping out or at least diminishing the injury by that satisfaction. The rule of justice here, he concludes, depends on the commandment against defrauding, not on the commandment against adultery. He weighs what the woman actually gets: chastity is a special treasure, but liberty is justly called an inestimable blessing, and so the terms were at least tolerable for her — the penalty of lust being that the conqueror should lose his booty. Wesley spells out what the prohibition on merchandise forbids, making gain of her either by using her for servile work or by prostituting her to the lusts or the service of others; and Gill notes only that the case supposed is of a man who tires of her some time after the marriage.
15:
Everyone treats the opening supposition as description rather than approval, and several go out of their way to say so. Gill says two wives are supposed but not approved, permitted for the hardness of men’s hearts, since it was not so from the beginning when one man and one woman were created and joined; the law is made only to prevent confusion and preserve order in families once the custom had taken hold. Wesley puts it in a line, that the practice is tolerated and not thereby made lawful, provision being made for the children and nothing more. Clarke agrees that polygamy existed under the Mosaic laws and was placed under regulation but never enjoined, Moses merely suffering it for hardness of heart, as our Lord remarks. Henry goes furthest, reading the verse as an exhibit against the practice: the law did not restrain it, probably in hope that men’s own experience of its inconvenience would at last end it and make them a law to themselves. Observe the supposition, he says — if a man have two wives it is a thousand to one but one is beloved and the other loved less, as Leah was by Jacob, and the effect cannot but be strife and jealousy, envy, confusion and every evil work, creating constant vexation to the husband and involving him in both sin and trouble; those consult their own ease far better who adhere to God’s law than those who indulge their lusts.

On the word hated there is no dispute at all. Clarke states the rule generally, that this is the true sense of the word in Scripture — loved less; so Jacob hated Leah, meaning he loved her less than Rachel, and so with the saying about Jacob loved and Esau hated, which he takes of a more particular affection shown to the one posterity than the other. Wesley and Henry give the same gloss in passing, comparatively, or manifestly loved less. Henry then draws out what he takes to be the point of the case as framed. Providence commonly sides with the weakest and gives more abundant honour to the part that lacked, and that is why the firstborn here is supposed to be the son of the less loved wife, as it fell out in Jacob’s family when the Lord saw that Leah was hated. The great householder wisely gives to each a dividend of comfort: if one woman had the honour of being the beloved wife, it often proved that the other had the honour of being the mother of the firstborn.
16: Calvin classifies the law rather than moralising on it, and the classification does the work. Since it provides that a father shall not unjustly transfer to one son what belongs to another, it is a part and supplement of the commandment against stealing, whose substance is that every man’s rights be preserved to him; for a father who put another son in the place of the firstborn was unquestionably committing a kind of theft. He then explains why the law was needed at all, since a father rarely degrades his firstborn where all the sons have one mother. Where polygamy was allowed the husband’s mind inclined generally to the second wife — because, he argues, a man who had loved the first with true affection would have been content with her as the companion of his life and never thought of another — and once tired of the first he might be coaxed by the second’s blandishments into taking from the earlier children what belonged to them. Hence the remedy that bars the father’s power to alter the right of primogeniture; and though such a man might plead that he gave only what was his own, Calvin calls it ungodly arrogance to reject one whom God has deigned to honour, since he who claims to assign the birthright where he pleases almost claims the ability to create. He does not leave the bar absolute: where there was just cause for disinheriting a firstborn, another might be substituted, as Jacob showed. On the mechanics, Gill notes that the dividing may be by a will in writing, by word of mouth, or by a deed of gift actually bestowing the goods, and that to acknowledge the son means to own and declare him so both by the will and by the division — one Targum rendering it separate, that is, distinguish him from the rest and make it known to all. Keil states the substance of the right itself, which is a double portion of everything the father has, resting on the ground the verse itself gives, that this son is the beginning of his strength.
18:
Henry notices the order of the two laws and takes it for deliberate: having just provided that parents shall not deprive their children of their right, it was fit to provide next that children not withdraw the honour and duty owing to their parents, for there is no partiality in the divine law. Gill offers a different reason for the sequence, reporting the rabbinic view that the law follows the one on captive marriage because such marriages often produced refractory children, the stock example being Absalom, whose mother David was said to have taken in war. On the description itself the two are close. Gill has him stubborn in his nature and rebellious in his actions, living contrary both to the laws of God and to the instruction of his parents — what he should do he does not, what he should not do he does — and all this in the teeth of counsel, admonition and correction. Henry enters one exclusion before listing the same: no child was to fare the worse for weakness of capacity or slowness of understanding, but only for wilfulness and obstinacy. The offender carries himself proudly toward his parents, contemns their authority, slights their reproofs, disobeys the commands they give for his own good, hates to be reformed by their correction, shames their family, grieves their hearts and threatens their estate by riotous living. Clarke does not soften the sentence and does not want it softened: severe as the law may seem, it must have acted as a powerful preventive of crime, and he adds the wish that if it were in force now and duly executed, how many deaths of disobedient and profligate children there would be in every corner of the land.

Calvin reads the law as generalising what had been said piecemeal before. By rebellious children are meant all who are abusive to father and mother, and if disobedience is capital then striking them or assailing them with reproaches is more so; from which, he observes, we learn what honouring father and mother actually means, since the punishment is denounced only for transgression of that commandment. But the weight of his comment falls on the procedure, which he calls an admirable means of moderating the severity of the law: God requires the case to be decided on the evidence of both parents and commands that it be publicly heard, so that no one is condemned at the will of private persons. He sets this against Roman practice, where a father held the power of life and death and might expose an infant, or imprison, scourge or put to death a grown child by whatever punishment he chose. Roman fathers, he grants, called friends into council before punishing; but the walls of a private dwelling conceal many disgraceful things, and God imposed a better restraint by not suffering parents to go beyond laying the information and giving testimony. Keil states the same double aim in a sentence: these laws defend parental authority and at the same time limit it.

The requirement that both parents act is where the protection is felt to lie. Gill records the rabbinic rule that if the father is willing to bring him to justice and the mother is not, or the reverse, he is not reckoned a stubborn and rebellious son at all until the two agree. Wesley gives the reason: the consent of both is required to prevent the abuse of this law to cruelty, and it cannot reasonably be supposed that both would agree except on incorrigible wickedness — in which case, he thinks, it is a righteous law, since rebellion against his own parents showed what a pernicious member of the commonwealth a man would be who had dissolved all his natural obligations. He adds a second safeguard: bringing him to the elders was itself a caution against the malice of hard-hearted parents.
20:
The charge is short, and Gill notes what tradition added to it. The parents speak in open court, and according to one Targum they preface the accusation by confessing their own sin, saying they have transgressed the decree of the word of the Lord in that such a son has been born to them. Wesley reads the two named vices as representative rather than exhaustive, gluttony and drunkenness standing for others of like or worse nature. Keil takes them the other way round, as the explanation of what precedes: these last accusations show the reason for the unmanageableness and the refractoriness.

Whether the son was tried before he was stoned is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, and the text gives each side something. Keil states the case for no trial at all. Nothing is said about evidence for the charge, or about a judicial inquiry of any kind; the elders are not regarded here as judges in the strict sense; and he quotes with approval the judgment that the charge was a proof in itself, since if the heart of a father and mother could be brought to the point of giving up their own child before the assembled community, everything had been done that a judge would need to know. What the law achieves, on his reading, is a transfer rather than an inquiry: the right of putting an incorrigible son to death passes from the parents to the town, while their authority is left intact. Calvin argues the opposite from the same silence. The sentence follows the accusation immediately, but we must infer that the judges pronounced it before the stoning, since otherwise they would be sitting there like ciphers; and the very mention of a trial implies the son was heard in his own defence, so that he might clear himself if not guilty. He then lists what such a hearing was for, and the list is a catalogue of the ways the law could be abused: the moroseness of the parents might be notorious; the father might be accusing the son at a stepmother’s instigation; some unworthy spite might come to light; the parents might have conspired against him in a fit of passion. It would be more than absurd, he says, that a son should be condemned unheard; and since he was to be stoned by the whole people he must first be convicted, which is why he was brought out publicly to plead his cause. Wesley stands with Calvin and puts it plainly: the elders were first to examine the cause with all exactness and then to pronounce sentence.

On the execution and its aftermath the reports diverge again. Gill describes a graduated procedure, the stoning following only after trial and sentence, and not until the son had been admonished and beaten before three judges, so that the parents could say in court that this was the son beaten in their presence; and he passes on a Targum that allows the whole thing to be halted, since if the son feared God and showed any token of repentance, and his parents wished to preserve him alive, they preserved him. He then records the tradition that settles the practical question: the Jews say this law, like that of retaliation, was never actually put into execution. Calvin reads the closing clause as naming a double purpose, that the earth should be purged of the sins by which it was in a manner polluted, and that the offender’s death should stand as an example; and he draws from the two named vices a point about the threshold: although men addicted to other vices were condemned too, Moses names these to show that dissolute profligacy was enough even where no capital crime could be alleged, since those are in a desperate state who have so cast away shame that their parents’ admonitions do them no good.
22:
What the hanging is, in relation to the death penalty, is settled the same way by two of them. Keil states that what is in view is not the hanging of criminals as the means of putting them to death, but the hanging of men already executed with the sword, so that the hanging is an intensification of the death penalty, the body being thereby exposed to peculiar abominations. Wesley says the same in one line, that it was done after the malefactor had been put to death some other way, this public shame being added to his former punishment. Gill takes the opening clause as covering any capital offence whatever, the rabbis restricting the phrase to the recognised modes of execution — strangling, the sword, burning and stoning — rather than to the case of the rebellious son just dealt with. Keil glosses the Hebrew behind a sin worthy of death as literally a right of death, that is, a capital crime.

Calvin sets out why a rule about corpses belongs in a law code at all, and his answer is about the living rather than the dead. The object of the precept was to banish inhumanity and barbarism from the chosen people, and to impress on them a horror even of a just execution; the body of a man suspended on a cross is a sad and hideous spectacle. He gives two grounds for the rights of burial themselves: they are a pledge and symbol of the resurrection, and they spare the eyes of the living from being defiled by the sight of so horrible a thing. He is careful that Moses is not speaking generally here but only of malefactors who are unworthy of the honour of burial — and yet even in their case the public good is regarded, lest men grow accustomed to cruelty and so become readier to commit murder. That is also how he reads the warning about the land: such inhumanity pollutes and disgraces it, and this was the more intolerable in a country God had given as an inheritance to his elect people, that he might be worshipped there purely with every profanation excluded.

On what God is and is not sanctioning, Calvin draws a line the others do not draw. God does not forbid criminals to be crucified or hanged on a gallows — he rather gives his sanction to this mode of punishment — and so it is not the penalty he disapproves; what he does by his own example is exhort the Israelites to abhor all atrocity, saying that he abominates those hanged on a tree so that the scandal may be removed at once. And the word accursed, on his reading, is not a verdict on the man’s soul: God does not call such men accursed as though their salvation were to be despaired of, but because the hanging was a mark of his curse. Calvin then names where the phrase is going, that Paul applies this passage to Christ, to teach us that he was made a curse for us that he might deliver us from the curse.
23:
The rule about the same day is reported with its practice attached. Gill insists it applies to everyone hanged and not only to the rebellious son, cites the account that such a man was stoned outside the city, left a whole day as a spectacle and buried at night, and then narrows the timing: the body was not to remain on the tree for any part of the night but to be taken down at sunset, one Targum reading the command as bury him at sunset and a rabbinic authority directing that a man be hanged near sunset and loosed immediately. He adds that the rule was not confined to those executed by the court, since anyone who left his dead unburied a night transgressed — unless he kept the body for its own honour, to procure a coffin and shroud. Clarke reads the one day of exposure as deliberately measured: it answered all the ends of public justice and exposed the shame and infamy of the conduct, without putting the feelings of humanity to torture by requiring a permanent exhibition of a human being left to putrefy. He then turns the verse against the practice of his own day, asking whether the spiking of the heads of state criminals ever prevented high treason, or the gibbeting of a thief ever prevented robbery, answering both in the negative and calling for the remains of that ancient barbarism to be banished with all possible speed. His verdict on the law as a whole is that in the punishments Moses prescribes mercy walks hand in hand with judgment.

What accursed of God means divides them by degrees, and the differences are real. Henry takes it at its lowest: the phrase signifies the highest degree of disgrace and reproach, since those who see a man hanging between heaven and earth will conclude him abandoned by both and unworthy of either; and he holds that Moses, by the Spirit, used the words when he meant no more than that a man was being treated most disgracefully, precisely so that they might afterward be applied to the death of Christ. Wesley takes it at its highest: the man is in a singular manner cursed and punished by God’s own appointment with a death held shameful among the Jews and all nations — and that, he argues, is enough by itself, so that lying unburied need not be added to it. Clarke puts it legally: the man has forfeited his life to the law, since cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in the book of the law, and in the execution of the sentence the curse was considered as alighting on his body, whence the necessity of removing the accursed thing out of sight. Calvin threads between them, allowing the phrase real force as a mark of God’s curse while denying that it despairs of the man’s salvation. Keil gives the clause and the reason without expounding either, letting the prohibition and the defilement of the land stand as they are written.

All of them see where the phrase is going. Wesley says the curse is appropriated to the hanged in order to signify that Christ should undergo this execrable punishment and be made a curse for us, and adds a point about time, that although the event was future in respect of men it was present to God. Henry makes the same connection the reason for the wording itself, that it might show how in his death Christ underwent the curse of the law for us, which proves his love and encourages faith in him. Calvin names the apostle who makes the application. Wesley also offers two readings of the defilement, either inhumanity toward the dead or the leaving in public view of a monument of the man’s wickedness and God’s curse, which should rather be buried in oblivion.
